full_judgment:
14. The limitation period, in case of a special law, is purported to be strictly applied and it would have been the same here if the VAT on the imported raw rubber was levied under the VAT Act, 1991. The HS Code No. 40.01, of the First Schedule to the VAT Act, 1991 (Act 22 of 1991) exempts import of raw rubber from VAT and there is nothing about VAT in the Customs Act. Therefore, the customs authority was not authorised by law to realise VAT on the imported raw rubber. It appears that mistake of law has led to the realisation of VAT on the imported raw rubber and the petitioner was compelled to pay, by the authority, under the VAT Act, 1991. The mistake is in thinking that the VAT levied was due when, in fact, it was not due and was realised illegally. In the case reported in 1949 AIR (PC) 297 it was held that if it is once established that the payment, even though it be of a tax, has been made by a party under mistake of law, that party is entitled to recover the same and the party refusing the same is bound to pay or return it. Since that decision, this view has been consistently followed by different courts of this subcontinent. 

 15. The fact being that VAT levied on the raw rubber, imported by the petitioner, was not authorised by law, the custom authorities cannot resort to the law in refusing to refund money, realised mistakenly as VAT, on grounds of limitation provided therein, simply for the reason that while levying VAT on the item they did not act under the same law. The authorities concerned had acted without jurisdiction. Their attempt to invoke section 33 of the Customs Act and section 67(1) of the VAT Act and seeking protection under them is fraught with misconception of law and should not have been insisted upon. The money thus realised by the customs authorities does not belong to the state and not retainable by it. It belongs to the petitioner who has a right to have it refunded by the respondents.
